title: Identifying critical lysines in mammalian histone H3 with high-throughput CRISPR prime editing.
data_url: https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41588-026-02675-y/MediaObjects/41588_2026_2675_MOESM3_ESM.xlsx (Supplementary Tables); GEO GSE319059, GSE319420, GSE319506; SRA PRJNA1268213

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed 10 supplementary/source-data Excel files (MOESM3-10, 15, 18; 11 KB to 3.0 MB). Counted: Supplementary Table 1 lists 57 prime-editing guide RNAs (epegRNAs) with spacer and extension sequences; figure source data for the lysine screen covers 12 H3 lysine sites (sheets 6c/6d, 72 numbers each; 6e/6f, 280 clone-level editing percentages each); sheet 8f holds raw RNA counts for 35,333 genes across 12 samples; sheet 8g holds differential-expression results for 5,967 genes across 4 genotypes; sheet 7g holds 12,472 single-guide RNAs over 1,219 genes. Checked GEO via NCBI esummary: GSE319059 = 12 RNA-seq samples, GSE319420 = 26 CUT&Tag samples, GSE319506 = 4 CUT&RUN samples.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That sheet 7g is a reanalysis of a previously published CRISPR knockout screen (the paper's reference 39), not data generated here; that epegRNAs were designed with DeepPrime v3.6 and PrimeDesign v0.2; that fitness was inferred from the difference in editing efficiency and PAM-only mutation accumulation between lysine-to-arginine and silent lysine-to-lysine conditions. Europe PMC's supplementary-file endpoint timed out (supplement not retrievable that way), so files came from the publisher's static-content URLs. Raw sequencing (SRA) not downloaded, per the no-raw-data rule.

a1_downloadable.note: All source-data Excel files downloaded without login (largest 3.0 MB); GEO series metadata public. Verified by opening the files.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: For the best candidate task, editing efficiency (% of sequencing reads carrying the intended change) is a column in the source data. The fitness label itself, however, is inferred from a lysine-to-arginine versus silent-control difference, so that variant would fail A2.

a3_inputs_present.note: Guide RNA spacer and extension sequences are present verbatim in Supplementary Table 1 (57 rows), so no identifier lookups are needed for the editing-efficiency task.

a4_units_stated.note: Percent of reads, percent indels, percent PAM-only are labelled in sheet headers; figure legends state replicate structure. Units partly implied in the western-blot sheets (relative signal, arbitrary units).

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL. Verified in the files: 57 epegRNAs total, only 12-13 lysine sites, 12 pooled measurements per condition, ~280 clone-level editing values, 12 RNA-seq samples over 4 genotypes. Every label this paper produced sits far below the ~1,500-row (or ~400 for classification) bar. The only tables with thousands of rows are gene-level RNA-seq outputs whose independent unit is 4 genotypes, and a 12,472-guide table that is a reanalysis of someone else's published screen.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~3.6 MB of Excel plus optional bigwig tracks
a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially laptop-sized; verified file sizes on disk.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: 13 lysine residues claimed, 12 sites in the screen source data (H3K4 reported separately); GEO sample counts match the described experiments. No contradictions found.

a8_label_provenance.note: Editing efficiencies are real amplicon-sequencing measurements, not model outputs. Note the 12,472-guide table comes from a different published screen, and fitness is an inferred quantity rather than a direct measurement.

existing_models.name: DeepPrime (deep-learning predictor of prime-editing guide RNA efficiency; used by this paper's authors to design their guides)
existing_models.score_and_split: Trained on 259,000 prime-editing guide RNAs across multiple editing systems and cell types; performance reported to plateau above ~180,000 training points (from search results, not re-run here).

existing_models.name: PRIDICT / DTMP-prime / PrimeNet (further published prime-editing efficiency predictors found in search)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved in detail; all are trained on library-scale measurements of tens to hundreds of thousands of guides.

backbone.name: Nucleotide Transformer or DNABERT-2 (DNA language models) would fit guide sequences; ESM-2 (protein language model) would fit histone residues

integration.partner_dataset: DeepPrime's 259,000-guide training library, or public oncohistone variant screens (e.g. the 2026 303-oncohistone multiomic screen)
integration.join_key: Guide spacer sequence / histone residue position
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does prime-editing efficiency learned from library-scale screens transfer to the highly repetitive, multi-copy histone gene cluster? — a real question, but 57 guides is far too few to answer it.

controls.positive_control: Would be: recover the known depletion of guides targeting Kat7 and Dot1l, and the textbook requirement for H3K4 and H3K9 methylation.
controls.negative_control: Silent lysine-to-lysine guides are built into the design, which is a genuinely good internal control.
controls.external_validation: DeepPrime's published library, and published mouse embryonic stem cell histone-mutant studies.

honest_claim_h3: With 57 guide RNAs and 12 lysine sites from one mouse embryonic stem cell line in one laboratory, no model trained here could claim more than 'fits these 57 guides'; nothing generalisable can be stated.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a prime-editing guide RNA's sequence to predict how efficiently it installs a lysine-to-arginine change in histone H3 genes.
plain_idea.train_on: The guide's spacer and extension sequence plus the local target sequence; 57 guides exist in Supplementary Table 1, of which only about 24 have matched efficiency measurements. Verified by opening the file.
plain_idea.predict: Percent of sequencing reads carrying the intended edit (and the percent with only the silent PAM change), measured by amplicon sequencing of the edited cell pools and clones.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Chromatin biologists editing multi-copy histone genes would like to know in advance which guides work in repetitive clusters, where existing predictors were never trained; but this paper supplies nowhere near enough guides to learn that.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: predict prime-editing efficiency in repetitive histone gene clusters from guide RNA sequence (57 guides), or predict which genes change expression under histone lysine-to-arginine mutation (5,967 genes but only 4 genotypes x 3 replicates). Both die on sample size; the second would also need all its features imported from external chromatin datasets, since the table carries only gene symbols.

effort.compute_note: Estimated from the actual downloaded files: 3.6 MB of Excel, 57 guide sequences; anything here runs in seconds on a laptop. The constraint is data volume, not compute.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows in Supplementary Table 1 and the lysine screen source data — 57 guides and 12 sites, done in ten minutes, and that is the whole answer.

verdict_reason: Fails A5 on verified counts. This is an elegant small-scale experimental paper, not a dataset: 57 prime-editing guide RNAs, 12-13 histone H3 lysine sites, ~280 clone-level editing measurements, and 12 RNA-seq samples across 4 genotypes. The large-looking tables are either gene-level outputs of a 4-condition experiment (5,967 genes, 12 samples) or a reanalysis of another paper's CRISPR screen (12,472 guides). For the one task the data genuinely fits — predicting prime-editing efficiency from guide sequence — DeepPrime was trained on roughly 259,000 guides, four orders of magnitude more than is available here.
